title: Calipers
description: Tool used to measure dimensions of an object
wiki_lead:
Calipers or callipers are an instrument used to measure the linear dimensions of an object or hole; namely, the length, width, thickness, diameter or depth of an object or hole. The word caliper comes from a corrupt form of caliber.
Many types of calipers permit reading out a measurement on a ruled scale, a dial, or an electronic digital display. A common association is to calipers using a sliding vernier scale.
Some calipers can be as simple as a compass with inward or outward-facing points, but with no scale (measurement indication). The tips of the caliper are adjusted to fit across the points to be measured, and then kept at that span while moved to separate measuring device, such as a ruler, or simply transferred directly to a workpiece.
Calipers are used in many fields such as mechanical engineering, metalworking, forestry, woodworking, science and medicine.
wiki_excerpt:
Calipers or callipers are an instrument used to measure the linear dimensions of an object or hole; namely, the length, width, thickness, diameter or depth of an object or hole. The word caliper comes from a corrupt form of caliber.
Many types of calipers permit reading out a measurement on a ruled scale, a dial, or an electronic digital display. A common association is to calipers using a sliding vernier scale.
Some calipers can be as simple as a compass with inward or outward-facing points, but with no scale (measurement indication). The tips of the caliper are adjusted to fit across the points to be measured, and then kept at that span while moved to separate measuring device, such as a ruler, or simply transferred directly to a workpiece.
Calipers are used in many fields such as mechanical engineering, metalworking, forestry, woodworking, science and medicine.


Terminology
Caliper is the American spelling, while calliper (double "L") is the British spelling.
A single tool might be referred to as a caliper or as calipers – a plural only (plurale tantum) form, like scissors or glasses.
Colloquially, the phrase "pair of verniers" or just "vernier" might refer to a vernier caliper. In loose colloquial usage, these phrases may also refer to other kinds of calipers, although they involve no vernier scale. In machine-shop usage, the term "caliper" is often used in contradistinction to micrometer, even though outside micrometers are a form of caliper. In this usage, caliper implies only the form factor of the instrument.


History

The earliest caliper has been found in the Greek Giglio wreck near the Italian coast. The ship's find dates to the 6th century BC. The wooden piece already featured a fixed and a movable jaw. Although rare finds, calipers remained in use by the Greeks and Romans.
A bronze caliper, dating from 9 AD, was used for minute measurements during the Chinese Xin dynasty. The caliper had an inscription stating that it was "made on the gui-you day, the first day of the first month of the first year of Shijianguo." The calipers included a "slot and pin" and "graduated in inches and tenths of an inch."
The modern vernier caliper was invented by Pierre Vernier, as an improvement of the nonius of Pedro Nunes.


Types


Inside caliper

Inside calipers are used to measure the internal size of an object.

The upper caliper in the image (on the right) requires manual adjustment prior to fitting. Fine setting of this caliper type is performed by tapping the caliper legs lightly on a handy surface until they will almost pass over the object. A light push against the resistance of the central pivot screw then spreads the legs to the correct dimension and provides the required, consistent feel that ensures a repeatable measurement.
The lower caliper in the image has an adjusting screw that permits it to be carefully adjusted without removal of the tool from the workpiece.


Outside caliper

Outside calipers are used to measure the external size of an object.
The same observations and technique apply to this type of caliper, as for the inside caliper. With some understanding of their limitations and usage, these instruments can provide a high degree of accuracy and repeatability. They are especially useful when measuring over very large distances; consider if the calipers are used to measure a large-diameter pipe. A vernier caliper does not have the depth capacity to straddle this large diameter and at the same time reach the outermost points of the pipe's diameter. They are made from high-carbon steel.


Divider caliper

In the metalworking field, a divider caliper, popularly called a compass, is used to mark out locations. The points are sharpened so that they act as scribers; one leg can then be placed in the dimple created by a center or prick punch and the other leg pivoted so that it scribes a line on the workpiece's surface, thus forming an arc or circle.
Their namesake use is in dividing a workpiece of arbitrary width
grok_lead: Calipers are precision measuring instruments designed to accurately determine the linear dimensions of an object, such as its length, width, thickness, diameter, or depth, by positioning two adjustable jaws or points against opposite sides. These tools are essential in fields requiring exact measurements, including engineering, manufacturing, machining, and scientific research, where they enable the assessment of internal and external features with resolutions as fine as 0.02 mm or 0.001 inches. Unlike basic rulers, calipers incorporate scales or digital displays to minimize human error and provide repeatable precision. The history of calipers traces back to ancient origins, with early sliding versions appearing in China during the reign of Wang Mang in A.D. 9, evolving from rudimentary scales used since around 1400 B.C. in various civilizations. A significant advancement came in 1631 when French mathematician Pierre Vernier invented the vernier scale, which enhanced measurement accuracy by allowing finer graduations on a secondary sliding scale. The first vernier calipers were produced in France around 1840 and in the United States in 1851 by Joseph R. Brown at Brown & Sharpe, marking the tool's industrialization. Post-World War II innovations introduced dial calipers in the 1960s for easier reading via analog dials, followed by digital calipers in the 1980s, pioneered by companies like Mitutoyo, which integrated electronic displays and data output for modern applications. Common types of calipers include vernier calipers, which rely on a manual sliding scale for analog precision; dial calipers, featuring a geared dial for quick visual readings; and digital calipers, offering electronic displays with absolute or incremental measurements and resolutions up to 0.01 mm. Specialized variants encompass inside calipers for internal diameters, outside calipers for external dimensions, depth calipers with probe extensions, and oddleg calipers for marking or gauging from an edge. In practice, calipers are widely employed in quality control to verify tolerances in machined parts, in automotive maintenance for component sizing, and in scientific experiments for precise sample analysis, ensuring compliance with standards like those from the Japanese Industrial Standards (JIS) established in 1954.
